text_blocks.snippet: Alexander Graham Bell was awarded the first official U.S. patent for the electric telephone on March 7, 1876.

list.snippet: First Call: On March 10, 1876, Bell successfully transmitted speech to his assistant, Thomas Watson, saying the famous words: “Mr. Watson—come here—I want to see you.”
The Patent: Bell applied for U.S. Patent 174,465 on February 14, 1876, just hours before competitor Elisha Gray filed a similar design caveat.
Public Debut: The invention was widely introduced to the public in June 1876 at the Centennial Exposition in Philadelphia.
Original Goal: Bell was originally attempting to improve the telegraph by sending multiple messages over a single wire using harmonic tones before discovering how to transmit voice.
Antonio Meucci: Developed an early voice-communication device called a teletrofono in the 1840s/1850s, leading to long-standing disputes over who truly made the first phone.
Philipp Reis: Constructed an early sound-transmitting device in 1861 that could send musical tones and simple sounds.
Thomas Edison: Later invented the carbon microphone, which greatly improved signal strength and made long-distance calls practical.
